messages:
alex_chen: hey — seeing a customer hit intermittent 429s and billing spikes. they say it started after a load test. unclear whether the limit is org-wide or per-project/api-key. any quick checks?

support_jenn: can you paste the raw response headers from one of the 429s? that tells us which limiter fired (X-RateLimit-* or Retry-After). also need the api key id if they can share (or masked).

alex_chen: pasted below (sanitized):

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Date: Tue, 11 Jun 2024 14:12:03 GMT
Content-Type: application/json
X-RateLimit-Limit: 60000
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1718004700
Retry-After: 45
{
  "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded", "type": "rate_limit" }
}

alex_chen: the customer is using a single project with multiple microservices, all sharing the same API key via a secrets store. they run egress through a NAT with a single IP.

maria_gonzalez: aha — two likely contributors: 1) API key concurrency or project-level quota reached, 2) IP-based enforcement because of the shared NAT. both can produce similar 429s but different scoping.

samir_k: quick distinction: if the X-RateLimit-Limit looks like a single large number that matches their subscription, it's probably org/project quota. if we were applying IP-level caps, we'd often include an X-RateLimit-Scope or the error body will say "ip_quota_exceeded" (not always consistent though).

support_jenn: from the headers you pasted, Remaining=0 and Reset timestamp — that looks like a token/api-key or project counter. but NAT'd IPs can exhaust per-IP bucket faster because all services share one source IP. ask customer: do any services use different API keys?

alex_chen: they confirmed only one API key. they tried rotating to a new key and saw immediate success for ~30s then 429 again.

maria_gonzalez: that pattern suggests a per-project or org quota (rotating keys won't help if quotas are attached to the project/org). if rotating fixed it for a short time, maybe the SDK had cached concurrency and some in-flight requests cleared.

support_jenn: repro checklist for us to triage quickly:
1) get a minimal curl that reproduces the 429 and include "-i" to capture headers. e.g.
```
curl -i -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \ 
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-REDACTED" \ 
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ 
  -d '{"model":"gpt-redwood-1","input":"hello"}'
```
2) run from the customer's NAT IP and from a different IP (home laptop) to compare.
3) if possible, create a new project in their org and a fresh key — see if quotas follow the org.
4) grab application logs showing request rate pattern and timestamps.

samir_k: also check auth edge cases: if they use short-lived session tokens and a few workers simultaneously request new tokens during expired-key spikes, that can cause bursts in upstream calls (token server + Redwood) and blow past soft limits. ask if they use token refresh loops.

alex_chen: customer says they use a token broker that refreshes keys every 60s and all 12 workers refresh within the same second during rolling deploys. that sounds bad.

maria_gonzalez: yep — thundering herd. recommend: stagger refresh jitter, exponential backoff, and a shared local cache so only one worker refreshes at a time.

support_jenn: immediate mitigations we gave the customer:
- add client-side 429 handler with exponential backoff + jitter (base 200ms, factor 2, max 60s)
- respect Retry-After header; for 429 always retry after that many seconds with jitter
- if using shared NAT, provision multiple egress IPs or split traffic across keys/projects so the per-ip bucket doesn't get exhausted
- avoid simultaneous key rotations/refreshes across many workers

alex_chen: they asked whether Redwood enforces any IP-based default limits for hosted accounts (they're on hosted API with pay-as-you-go).

support_jenn: short answer: we apply a combination of scopes. there are default soft limits at the API-key/project level and protective per-IP rate controls (to protect the platform). enterprise Dedicated/Dedicated+Reserved customers can request custom limits and IP allowlists. for hosted payg accounts, the system will surface X-RateLimit headers; if IP-based mitigation triggered, the error body sometimes references "source_ip" or we surface a friendly note in the dashboard.

maria_gonzalez: if customer needs sustained burst capacity, recommend they either: 1) upgrade to a higher plan / reserved capacity (if available), or 2) split high-rate workloads across multiple project keys and route them evenly (and still implement backoff). both need ops coordination.

samir_k: internal triage notes for us to escalate if needed:
- check org-level quota and billing spikes in billing console for that org id between first_message_ts and last_message_ts.
- look at ingress logs for the NAT IP to see aggregate QPS and which API key IDs were present.
- correlate with any recent deploys from the customer (rolling restarts often cause bursts).
- if we see repeated bursts that exceed platform IP protection thresholds, we can temporarily raise the IP bucket for their IP while they remediate, but require ops approval.

alex_chen: customer also reported intermittent 401s earlier in the day when rotating secrets — could 401s lead to retries that cause subsequent 429s?

support_jenn: absolutely. common pattern: 401 -> client retries immediately and reauths -> reauth path triggers extra requests (token server + repeated failed requests) -> sudden burst. recommend instrumenting client to throttle reauth attempts: exponential backoff + single-flight dedupe so only one reauth in flight per process.

maria_gonzalez: we should also advise customers to watch both the API token usage and egress IP QPS. SRE note: add a dashboard for suspected NAT-saturated IPs per org so support can triage faster.

support_jenn: i've opened a support ticket for this org and attached the headers/log snippet. I've recommended the immediate mitigations and requested logs. asking ops to check quota buckets and consider a temporary IP bucket increase if we confirm platform protection triggered.

ops-bot: Incident ticket #INC-5231 created and assigned to eng-sre. ETA for initial review: 2 hours. :white_check_mark:

alex_chen: thanks — i'll relay mitigations to the customer and ask them to run the repro steps. will post results here.

(added later) alex_chen: customer ran curl from home laptop — saw no 429, but from their prod NAT IP they get 429 within ~30s of high-concurrency test. they agreed to stagger token refresh and add client backoff for now.

support_jenn: closing loop: likely root cause = shared NAT IP + thundering refresh + project-level quota. mitigation plan looks good. if they still need sustained high concurrency, advise upgrading to reserved capacity or splitting into multiple projects and keys.

samir_k: +1 — also remind them to check library versions; older SDKs can aggressively retry without jitter.

alex_chen: nice, thanks all. i'll follow up if it reappears. :raised_hands:
